comparison: Both strongly support the core LOVdeg design and validation (C40-C55, C106). OpenEval emphasizes the structural analysis and mutation strategy, while peer reviewers highlight the 'convincing methodology' and 2-20x degradation levels. Both agree this is a valuable tool addition.

Perfect agreement on mechanistic validation (C56-C57). Both acknowledge the protease knockout studies and control experiments. Peer Reviewer 2 notes the mechanism is ClpA-dominated but not completely verified, while OpenEval emphasizes these controls rule out artifacts like light toxicity.

Strong agreement on dose-response, timing, and SsrA comparison (C58-C60). OpenEval notes limitations in direct SsrA comparison due to temporal dynamics. Peer reviewers confirm comparable kinetics to other optogenetic systems and several-fold protein reduction. Peer R3 also includes microscopy data (C61) that OpenEval addresses separately in R4.

OpenEval R4 addresses microscopy control ruling out aggregation (C61), which peer reviewers implicitly accept as part of their broader validation in R3. No explicit peer challenge to this control experiment.

Both support LacI modularity demonstration (C62-C64). OpenEval groups all three modularity applications together (LacI, CRISPRa, AcrB), while peer reviewers address each separately. Both acknowledge incomplete reversal but find evidence convincing. Peer R4 focuses specifically on LacI, confirming indirect but convincing measurement.

Both support CRISPRa modularity (C65-C66). OpenEval includes this in broader modularity assessment, while peer reviewers note it's 'seemingly less effective than mCherry degradation.' Both acknowledge incomplete reversal without considering it a fundamental limitation.

Both strongly support AcrB/efflux pump modularity (C72-C76). OpenEval emphasizes chloramphenicol sensitivity assays demonstrating functional degradation. Peer reviewers describe this as 'most compelling data' showing fusion without affecting original protein function. Both confirm modularity claim C2.

Strong agreement on V416I variant and frequency-dependent degradation (C82-C87). OpenEval emphasizes photocycle dynamics rationale and improved light sensitivity for bioreactor applications. Peer Reviewer 2 confirms the mutation slows reversion time, making LOVdeg more sensitive to short light pulses for low-light conditions.

Perfect agreement on multilayer control synergy (C3, C88-C92). OpenEval emphasizes faster kinetics and greater fold change from combined system. Peer reviewers confirm 23-fold decrease with combination vs 7-fold with LOVdeg alone, and note utility of pairing with existing optogenetic tools.

Strong agreement on metabolic engineering application (C4, C93-C105). Both confirm LOVdeg decreased octanoic acid production, EL222 alone was ineffective, and combination was most effective. Both support the interpretation that degradation is necessary for stationary phase control where transcriptional repression fails.

Partial overlap on advantages and broader applications (C107-C112). OpenEval rates these claims as UNCERTAIN, noting they represent speculative future applications not directly tested. Peer reviewers (R10) support the demonstrated complementarity and advantages (C108-C110) based on actual data, but don't explicitly address the more speculative future application claims (C111-C112).

OpenEval R10 addresses limitations (C113-C115) including degradation saturation, resource utilization, and portability questions. No corresponding peer review result explicitly discusses these limitations, though they are implicitly accepted as part of the authors' honest discussion.
OpenEval R11 validates background knowledge and prior work citations (C5-C39). Peer reviewers do not separately evaluate these background claims, implicitly accepting them as appropriate context.

OpenEval R12 validates established knowledge about AcrAB-TolC system and LOV photochemistry (C67-C71, C77-C81). Peer reviewers do not separately evaluate these background claims but use this knowledge in their assessments.
OpenEval R13 validates methodological details (C116-C120). Peer reviewers do not separately evaluate these procedural claims, focusing instead on results and interpretations.
